Objectives of the Study: 
After studying this unit, the student should be able to 
- 
understand the market structure Perfect Competition 
 
Perfect Competition 
Perfect competition is a common market structure that has very desirable properties, so it is 
useful to compare other market structures to competition. In this section, we describe the 
properties of competitive firms and markets. 
In general terms, competition refers to firms rivalling with one another to attract customers. 
However, in economics, a market is considered perfectly competitive only when firms are price 
takers, meaning they cannot influence market prices and must accept the price determined by 
market demand and supply. 
Perfect competition represents an ideal market situation where resources are allocated 
efficiently, and no individual buyer or seller has control over the price. 
I. Price Taking 
When most people talk about “competitive firms,” they usually refer to firms that compete or 
rival with one another to attract customers. In this general sense, any market with more than 

--- Page 2 ---
one firm may be considered competitive. However, in economics, the term “competitive 
market” has a more precise meaning. 
Economists define a market as competitive only when all firms within it are price takers. A 
price-taking firm is one that cannot influence the market price of its product or the prices of 
the inputs it uses. Instead, the price is determined by the overall interaction of market demand 
and supply, and each individual firm must accept this price. 
Why is a firm a price taker? 
A firm becomes a price taker because of the structure of the market in which it operates. In a 
perfectly competitive market: 
 
There are a large number of firms. 
 
Each firm produces only a very small portion of total output. 
 
Products are identical across firms. 
Due to these conditions, no single firm has enough market power to influence price. If one firm 
changes its output, the effect on total market supply is negligible, and therefore the market 
price remains unchanged. 
Role of the Demand Curve 
A key reason why firms are price takers is that they face a perfectly elastic (horizontal) demand 
curve at the prevailing market price. This has several important implications: 
 
The firm can sell any quantity of output at the given market price. 
 
The firm has no incentive to lower its price, because it can already sell all its output at 
the existing price. 
 
The firm cannot increase its price, because buyers would immediately switch to other 
sellers offering the same product. 
Infinitely Elastic Demand 
The demand curve faced by the firm is said to be infinitely elastic. This means: 
 
Even a very small increase in price leads to a complete loss of customers. 

--- Page 3 ---
 
At the market price, demand is perfectly responsive, allowing the firm to sell any 
quantity. 
For example, consider a farmer selling wheat in a large agricultural market. If the farmer tries 
to charge a higher price than others, buyers will simply purchase wheat from other farmers 
since all wheat is identical. As a result, the farmer has no control over price and must accept 
the prevailing market rate. 
II. Why the Firm’s Demand Curve Is Horizontal  
In a perfectly competitive market, the demand curve faced by an individual firm is perfectly 
elastic, meaning it is a horizontal straight line at the prevailing market price. This occurs 
because firms are price takers and cannot influence the price through their individual actions. 
The horizontal nature of the demand curve is not accidental; it is the result of several important 
characteristics of perfect competition. 
1. Large Number of Buyers and Sellers 
In a perfectly competitive market, there are a large number of buyers and sellers, each of whom 
is very small relative to the overall market. As a result: 
 
No single firm can influence the total market supply. 
 
Any change in the output of a single firm has a negligible effect on market price. 
For example, soybean farmers are price takers because each farmer produces only a tiny 
fraction of total output. Even if one farmer stops producing, the overall market supply changes 
very little, so the market price remains unaffected. 
Thus, each firm must accept the given market price, which leads to a horizontal demand curve. 
2. Identical (Homogeneous) Products 
All firms in perfect competition produce identical or homogeneous products. Consumers 
perceive no difference between goods supplied by different firms. 
 
A buyer does not care which firm supplies the product. 

--- Page 4 ---
 
If one firm charges a higher price, consumers will immediately switch to other sellers. 
For instance, agricultural products like apples or wheat are considered identical in quality. 
Because of this uniformity, no firm can charge a price above the market level. 
This forces firms to accept the market price, making the demand curve perfectly elastic. 
3. Full Information 
In a perfectly competitive market, buyers and sellers have complete knowledge about: 
 
Prices charged by all firms 
 
Product quality and characteristics 
This transparency ensures that: 
 
Buyers always purchase from the cheapest seller. 
 
Firms cannot charge higher prices without losing all customers. 
If a firm attempts to increase its price, consumers—being fully informed—will shift instantly 
to other firms. Hence, the firm’s demand drops to zero above the market price. 
4. Negligible Transaction Costs 
Transaction costs refer to the costs involved in buying or selling a product, such as time, 
transportation, or legal expenses. 
In perfect competition: 
 
These costs are very low or negligible. 
 
Buyers can easily switch from one seller to another without any inconvenience. 
For example, in commodity markets, buyers can quickly compare prices and make purchases 
with minimal effort. Because switching is so easy, even a slight increase in price by a firm will 
result in a complete loss of demand. This reinforces the horizontal shape of the demand curve. 
5. Free Entry and Exit of Firms 

--- Page 5 ---
Firms can freely enter or exit the market depending on profit conditions: 
 
If firms earn abnormal profits, new firms enter the market. 
 
Increased competition pushes prices down to the normal level. 
 
If firms incur losses, some firms exit, reducing supply and stabilizing prices. 
This process ensures that: 
 
No firm can sustain a higher price in the long run. 
 
Firms remain price takers at all times. 
A practical example of a nearly perfectly competitive market is the Chicago Mercantile 
Exchange. 
This market exhibits the following features: 
 
Thousands of buyers and sellers participate in trading. 
 
Products such as wheat and other commodities are standardized and identical. 
 
Prices are publicly available, ensuring full information. 
 
Transactions occur quickly with minimal cost. 
 
Entry and exit into trading are relatively easy. 
Because of these conditions, traders in such markets cannot influence prices individually and 
must accept the prevailing market price. 
Deviations from Perfect Competition  
In reality, very few markets satisfy all the strict conditions of perfect competition. Most markets 
deviate from this ideal structure in one way or another. However, even when these deviations 
exist, many markets still behave in a manner similar to perfectly competitive markets, 
especially when there are a large number of firms and strong competition. 
1. Government Restrictions on Entry 
In some markets, the government imposes restrictions that limit the entry of new firms. These 
restrictions may include: 

--- Page 6 ---
 
Licensing requirements 
 
Zoning laws 
 
Legal regulations 
Such barriers prevent completely free entry and exit, which is a key feature of perfect 
competition. However, if the number of existing firms is still large, individual firms may 
continue to behave as price takers because no single firm has significant control over price. 
2. Presence of Transaction Costs 
In the real world, transaction costs are rarely zero. Buyers and sellers may incur costs such as: 
 
Transportation expenses 
 
Search costs (finding the best price) 
 
Legal or administrative costs 
When transaction costs are high, consumers may not switch sellers even if there is a price 
difference. This gives some firms limited pricing power. However, if transaction costs are 
relatively low, markets can still function close to perfect competition. 
3. Incomplete or Imperfect Information 
Perfect competition assumes that all buyers and sellers have complete information about prices 
and products. In reality: 
 
Consumers may not know all available prices 
 
Information about product quality may be limited 
Despite this, even if only some buyers are well-informed, they can influence the market by 
choosing lower-priced sellers. This competitive pressure prevents firms from significantly 
increasing prices. 
4. Product Differentiation 
In many markets, products are not perfectly identical. Firms may differentiate their products 
through: 

--- Page 7 ---
 
Branding 
 
Quality differences 
 
Packaging 
This reduces the degree of competition and gives firms some control over pricing. However, if 
products are still close substitutes, competition remains strong. 
5. Limited Mobility of Resources 
Factors of production such as labor and capital may not move freely due to: 
 
Skill differences 
 
Geographical constraints 
 
Institutional barriers 
This restricts the flexibility assumed in perfect competition. Even so, in industries where 
mobility is relatively high, firms behave more like price takers. 
 
III. Derivation of a Competitive Firm’s Demand Curve  
The demand curve faced by an individual firm in a competitive market is derived from the 
concept of residual demand. Residual demand refers to the portion of total market demand that 
remains after accounting for the supply provided by all other firms in the market. 
In other words, a firm can only sell what other firms do not supply at a given price. 
Residual Demand Concept 
A firm faces a residual demand curve defined as: 
Dr(p) = D(p) - So(p) 
Where: 
 
Dr(p) = Residual demand for the firm 
 
D(p) = Total market demand 

--- Page 8 ---
 
So(p) = Supply of all other firms 
This equation shows that the demand available to an individual firm depends on both the total 
market demand and the quantity supplied by competing firms. 
The concept of residual demand can be understood step by step: 
 
A firm sells its product only to those consumers who have not already purchased from 
other firms. 
 
At high prices, other firms are willing to supply a large quantity. If their supply fully 
satisfies market demand, the residual demand for the firm becomes zero. 
 
At lower prices, other firms supply less than the total market demand. The remaining 
unmet demand becomes available to the individual firm. 
Thus, the firm’s demand is not the total market demand, but only the leftover demand after 
other firms have supplied their share. 
The residual demand curve is derived by comparing: 
 
The market demand curve, and 
 
The supply curve of other firms 
At each price level: 
 
Subtract the quantity supplied by other firms from total market demand. 
 
The remaining quantity represents the demand faced by the individual firm. 
Graphically, the residual demand curve is the horizontal difference between the market demand 
curve and the supply curve of other firms as shown in the figure 18.1. 
Figure 18.1: Residual Demand Curve 

--- Page 9 ---
 
The market demand that is not met by other sellers at any given price. The firm’s residual 
demand function, Dr(p), shows the quantity demanded from the firm at price p. A firm sells 
only to people who have not already purchased the good from another seller. We can determine 
how much demand is left for a particular firm at each possible price using the market demand 
curve and the supply curve for all other firms in the market. The quantity the market demands 
is a function of the price: 
Q = D(p) 
The supply curve of the other firms is So(p). The residual demand function equals the market 
demand function, D(p), minus the supply function of all other firms: 
Dr(p) = D(p) - So(p) 
At prices so high that the amount supplied by other firms, So(p), is greater than the quantity 
demanded by the market, D(p), the residual quantity demanded, Dr(p), is zero. In Figure 18.1 
we derive the residual demand for a Canadian manufacturing firm that produces metal chairs. 
Panel b shows the market demand curve, D, and the supply of all but one manufacturing firm, 
So. At p = $66 per chair, the supply of other firms, 500 units (where one unit is 1,000 metal 
chairs) per year, exactly equals the market demand (panel b), so the residual quantity demanded 
of the remaining firm (panel a) is zero. At prices below $66, the other chair manufacturers are 
not willing to supply as much as the market demands. At p = $63, for example, the market 
demand is 527 units, but other firms want to supply only 434 units. As a result, the residual 
quantity demanded from the individual firm at p = $63 is 93 (= 527 - 434) units. Thus, the 
residual demand curve at any given price is the horizontal difference between the market 
demand curve and the supply curve of the other firms. The residual demand curve the firm 
faces in panel a is much flatter than the market demand curve in panel b. As a result, the 
elasticity of the residual demand curve is much higher than the market elasticity. If the market 
has n identical firms, the elasticity of demand, εi, facing Firm i is 
εi = nε - (n - 1)ηo, 

--- Page 10 ---
where ε is the market elasticity of demand (a negative number), ηo is the elasticity of supply of 
each of the other firms (typically a positive number), and n - 1 is the number of other firms. As 
equation εi = nε - (n - 1)ηo shows, a firm’s residual demand curve is more elastic the more 
firms, n, are in the market, the more elastic the market demand, ε, and the larger the elasticity 
of supply of the other firms, ηo. The residual demand elasticity, εi, must be at least as elastic as 
nε if the supply curve slopes up so that the second term makes the estimate more elastic. Thus, 
using nε as an approximation is conservative. For example, even though the estimated market 
elasticity of demand for soybeans is very inelastic at about ε = -0.2, because n = 107,000, the 
residual demand facing a single soybean farm must be at least nε = 107,000 × (-0.2) = -21,400, 
which is extremely elastic. 
Thus, we can say that the residual demand curve has the following characteristics: 
 
It is flatter (more elastic) than the market demand curve. 
 
As the number of firms increases, each firm’s share of the market becomes smaller. 
 
Consequently, the residual demand curve becomes more elastic. 
 
In the case of a very large number of firms, the curve becomes perfectly horizontal, 
indicating perfectly elastic demand. 
This explains why firms in perfect competition are price takers. 
IV. Profit Maximization 
Economists generally assume that all firms aim to maximize profit. This assumption is based 
on two main reasons: 
 
Many businesspeople explicitly state that profit maximization is their objective. 
 
Firms that fail to maximize profit are likely to incur losses and eventually be forced out 
of the market. 
Thus, profit maximization is considered the primary goal of firms in economic theory. 
Meaning of Profit 
A firm’s profit π, is defined as the difference between its total revenue R and total cost C: 
π = R - C 

--- Page 11 ---
 
If (π > 0) → Profit 
 
If (π < 0) → Loss 
Economic Cost vs Business Cost 
Economists measure cost as opportunity cost, which includes: 
 
Explicit costs (wages, materials, rent) 
 
Implicit costs (forgone income, owner’s time) 
This leads to a difference between: 
 
Business profit (accounting profit) 
 
Economic profit 
Example: 
Suppose a person earns ₹20,000 from their own business. If they could earn ₹25,000 working 
elsewhere, then: 
 
Economic profit = 20,000 − 25,000 = –₹5,000 (loss) 
Thus, ignoring opportunity cost can lead to incorrect decisions. 
A firm must make two key decisions for profit maximisation: 
1. Output Decision 
What level of output q* maximizes profit? 
2. Shutdown Decision 
Should the firm produce or shut down? 
Profit Maximization Rules 
Rule 1: The firm produces the output level where profit is maximum. 
Rule 2: The firm produces where marginal profit = 0. 

--- Page 12 ---
Rule 3: MR(q) = MC(q) 
Where: 
 
MR = Marginal Revenue 
 
MC = Marginal Cost 
That is, 
 
If MR > MC → Increase output 
 
If MR < MC → Reduce output 
 
If MR = MC → Profit is maximized 
Shutdown Rule  
The shutdown rule is an important concept in economics that helps a firm decide whether it 
should continue production or temporarily cease operations in order to minimize losses. This 
decision depends on the relationship between the firm’s revenue and its costs, and it differs 
between the short run and the long run. 
In the short run, a firm faces two types of costs namely fixed costs and variable costs. Fixed 
costs, such as rent, machinery, and equipment, are considered sunk costs because they must be 
paid regardless of whether the firm produces any output. Since these costs cannot be recovered, 
they are irrelevant when making the shutdown decision. Instead, the firm focuses only on 
variable costs, which include expenses like wages, raw materials, and electricity—costs that 
can be avoided if production stops. If the firm’s total revenue is greater than or equal to its 
variable cost, it should continue producing, even if it is making an overall loss. This is because 
the firm is covering all its variable costs and contributing something toward its fixed costs, 
thereby reducing its total loss. However, if the firm’s revenue falls below its variable cost, it 
means that the firm cannot even cover the costs that could be avoided by shutting down. In 
such a situation, continuing production would increase losses, so the firm should temporarily 
shut down. So in the short run shut down only if:  Revenue < Variable Cost. 
In the long run, the shutdown decision becomes simpler because all costs are variable and 
avoidable. There are no fixed or sunk costs, as the firm has enough time to adjust all inputs, 
sell assets, or exit the industry completely. Therefore, the firm must ensure that its total revenue 

--- Page 13 ---
covers all its costs. If the firm is unable to do so and incurs any economic loss, it will choose 
to shut down and exit the market. Unlike in the short run, there is no justification for continuing 
production at a loss because all costs can be avoided. 
V. Short-Run Competitive Profit Maximization 
Meaning of Short Run  
The short run in economics refers to a period of time during which at least one factor of 
production remains fixed and cannot be changed. This fixed factor is usually capital, such as 
machinery, buildings, or equipment, which cannot be increased or reduced quickly due to time 
and cost constraints. Because of this limitation, firms can adjust only some inputs—like labor 
or raw materials—while others remain constant. In the short run, firms also cannot freely enter 
or exit the market. New firms cannot quickly enter because setting up production facilities takes 
time, and existing firms cannot completely leave the market since they are tied to fixed assets. 
However, they may choose to temporarily stop production if conditions are unfavourable. Thus, 
the short run is characterized by limited flexibility in production decisions and constraints on 
market participation. 
Output Decision in Short Run  
In the short run, a firm operating under perfect competition determines its level of output based 
on the goal of profit maximization. Since the firm is a price taker, it has no control over the 
market price and must accept the price determined by market demand and supply. As a result, 
the firm’s price (P) is equal to its marginal revenue (MR). This means that every additional 
unit sold adds the same amount to revenue, equal to the market price. Therefore, the profit-
maximizing condition for a competitive firm becomes: 
MC(q) = p 
This condition implies that the firm will adjust its level of output until its marginal cost (MC) 
equals the market price. If the marginal cost of producing an additional unit is less than the 
price (MC < P), the firm can increase its profit by producing more, because the revenue from 
selling that unit exceeds its cost. On the other hand, if the marginal cost is greater than the price 
(MC > P), the firm should reduce its output, as producing extra units would add more to cost 
than to revenue, thereby reducing profit. Profit is maximized only when MC = P, because at 

--- Page 14 ---
this point, the additional revenue from producing one more unit exactly equals the additional 
cost, and there is no further gain from changing output. Thus, in the short run, a competitive 
firm carefully adjusts its production level to this equilibrium condition in order to achieve 
maximum profit or minimum loss. 
Profit or Loss in the Short Run and Short-Run Supply Curve  
In the short run, a firm operating under perfect competition may find itself in different profit 
situations depending on market conditions and its cost structure. The firm may earn 
supernormal (abnormal) profit when its total revenue exceeds total cost, or normal profit when 
revenue just equals total cost, covering both explicit and implicit costs. However, the firm may 
also incur losses when total cost exceeds total revenue. Despite this possibility, a firm does not 
immediately shut down when it incurs losses in the short run. This is because fixed costs, such 
as rent and machinery, are unavoidable in the short run. As long as the firm’s revenue is 
sufficient to cover its variable costs, it will continue production, since doing so allows it to 
cover part of its fixed costs and thereby reduce overall losses. The firm will only shut down if 
its revenue falls below variable costs. 
The short-run supply curve of a competitive firm is derived from its marginal cost (MC) curve, 
but only the portion that lies above the average variable cost (AVC) curve. This is because the 
firm will produce only when price (which equals marginal revenue) is at least equal to AVC. 
If the price falls below AVC, the firm cannot cover its variable costs and will shut down. Thus, 
the MC curve above AVC represents the firm’s willingness to supply output at different price 
levels. 
The key insight from this analysis is that in the short run, firms have limited flexibility due to 
fixed costs. As a result, they may continue operating even when they are making losses, 
provided they can cover their variable costs. Fixed costs cannot be avoided in the short run, so 
firms focus on minimizing losses rather than immediately exiting the market. 
VI. Long-Run Competitive Profit Maximization 
Meaning of Long Run  
The long run in economics refers to a period of time sufficiently long for a firm to adjust all its 
factors of production. Unlike the short run, where at least one factor remains fixed, in the long 

--- Page 15 ---
run all inputs are variable, meaning firms can change the scale of production by increasing or 
decreasing labor, capital, machinery, and plant size. Because of this flexibility, firms can fully 
adapt to changes in market conditions. 
Another important feature of the long run is that firms can freely enter or exit the market. If 
existing firms are earning profits, new firms are attracted to the industry, increasing 
competition. On the other hand, if firms are incurring losses, some will leave the market. This 
process continues until only normal profits are earned. 
In the long run, no fixed costs remain, because all costs can be adjusted or avoided. Firms are 
not bound by past investments, and they can reorganize production or completely shut down if 
it is not profitable. As a result, the long run represents a period of full flexibility and adjustment, 
where firms make decisions that ensure efficiency and long-term sustainability. 
Output Decision in Long Run  
In the long run, a firm determines its level of output using the same fundamental profit-
maximization rule as in the short run. The firm aims to produce at the level where its marginal 
revenue (MR) equals marginal cost (MC), since this is the point at which profit is maximized. 
In a perfectly competitive market, the firm is a price taker, meaning it cannot influence the 
market price and must accept it as given. Therefore, the firm’s marginal revenue is equal to the 
market price. 
MR = MC 
Since: 
MR = P 
It follows that: 
MC = P 
This means that in the long run, the firm will adjust its output level until the marginal cost of 
producing an additional unit equals the market price. If the marginal cost is less than the price, 
the firm can increase profit by expanding production. If the marginal cost is greater than the 
price, the firm should reduce output to avoid losses. The equilibrium is reached when MC 

--- Page 16 ---
equals price, ensuring that the firm is producing the most efficient level of output. Thus, even 
in the long run, the condition MC = P remains the key rule guiding a competitive firm’s output 
decision. 
Shutdown Decision in Long Run  
The shutdown decision in the long run is relatively simple compared to the short run because 
all costs are variable and avoidable. Unlike the short run, there are no fixed or sunk costs that 
the firm is forced to bear. This means the firm has complete flexibility to adjust its inputs, scale 
of production, or even exit the market entirely. As a result, the firm must ensure that its total 
revenue is sufficient to cover all its costs in order to continue operating. 
If a firm finds that it is incurring any economic loss, meaning its total revenue is less than its 
total cost, it will choose to shut down and exit the market. Continuing production in such a 
situation would not be rational, since the firm can avoid all costs by ceasing operations. 
Therefore, in the long run, only firms that are able to earn at least normal profit (where revenue 
equals total cost) will remain in the market. Firms that fail to do so will exit, ensuring that 
resources are allocated efficiently over time. 
Long-Run Supply Curve  
In the long run, the supply curve of a perfectly competitive firm is derived from its long-run 
marginal cost (LRMC) curve, but only the portion that lies above the long-run average cost 
(LRAC) curve. This is because, in the long run, all costs are variable and the firm must cover 
all its costs to remain in business. The firm will choose to produce only when the market price 
is at least equal to its average cost; otherwise, it will incur losses and exit the market. 
A profit-maximizing firm determines its output where price equals marginal cost (P = MC). In 
the long run, this condition becomes P = LRMC, and the firm supplies output only if this price 
is also sufficient to cover the average cost. Therefore, the relevant portion of the LRMC curve 
is the segment that lies above the LRAC curve, as this ensures that the firm earns at least normal 
profit. 
If the market price is below the LRAC, the firm cannot cover its total costs and will shut down 
in the long run. On the other hand, if the price is equal to the minimum point of the LRAC 
curve, the firm earns zero economic profit (normal profit) and continues operating. Thus, the 

--- Page 17 ---
long-run supply curve reflects the firm’s willingness to supply output at different price levels 
while ensuring long-term sustainability and efficiency. 
Entry and Exit of Firms  
In a perfectly competitive market, the number of firms in the industry is determined by the 
processes of entry and exit, which occur in response to profit or loss. Entry of firms takes place 
when existing firms in the market are earning supernormal (abnormal) profits. These high 
profits act as an incentive for new firms to enter the industry, as they expect to earn similar 
returns. As new firms enter, the total market supply increases, which leads to a fall in market 
price and a reduction in profits. 
On the other hand, exit of firms occurs when firms in the market are incurring losses. Losses 
signal that resources are not being used efficiently, so some firms choose to leave the industry 
to avoid further losses. As firms exit, the total market supply decreases, which causes the 
market price to rise and reduces the losses of the remaining firms. 
This continuous process of entry and exit ensures that, in the long run, firms earn only normal 
profit (zero economic profit). It also helps maintain equilibrium in the market by adjusting 
supply in response to changes in profitability. 
Long-Run Equilibrium  
In a perfectly competitive market, long-run equilibrium is achieved when firms reach a position 
where price equals marginal revenue, marginal cost, and long-run average cost: 
P = MR = MC = LRAC 
At this point, firms are producing at the most efficient level of output, where the cost of 
producing an additional unit (MC) is exactly equal to the revenue earned from it (MR), and this 
is also equal to the market price. Since price is equal to long-run average cost (LRAC), firms 
are able to cover all their costs, including both explicit and implicit (opportunity) costs. 
One of the key implications of this equilibrium is that firms earn zero economic profit, also 
known as normal profit. This does not mean firms are making no money; rather, it means they 
are earning just enough to keep their resources in the current use, with no extra incentive for 

--- Page 18 ---
new firms to enter or existing firms to leave the market. As a result, there is no tendency for 
entry or exit, and the market remains stable. 
Another important implication is that the price equals the minimum point of the average cost 
curve, which indicates that firms are operating at the most efficient scale of production. This 
leads to an efficient allocation of resources, where goods are produced at the lowest possible 
cost and supplied at a price that reflects this efficiency. Thus, long-run equilibrium in perfect 
competition ensures both productive efficiency and overall economic efficiency in the market. 
Adjustment Process  
The adjustment process in a perfectly competitive market explains how the forces of entry and 
exit bring the market toward long-run equilibrium. When firms in the market are earning 
supernormal profits, it signals that the industry is highly profitable. This attracts new firms to 
enter the market, as they expect to earn similar profits. As more firms enter, the overall market 
supply increases, which leads to a fall in market price. This process continues until the extra 
profits are eliminated and firms earn only normal profit. 
On the other hand, when firms are incurring losses, it indicates that the market is not profitable. 
As a result, some firms exit the market to avoid further losses. The exit of firms reduces the 
total market supply, which in turn causes the market price to rise. This rise in price helps the 
remaining firms recover their costs. The process of exit continues until losses are eliminated 
and firms again earn normal profit. 
Thus, the adjustment process ensures that in the long run, the market stabilizes at a point where 
firms earn zero economic profit, with no incentive for further entry or exit. 
Conclusion 
In conclusion, the concept of perfect competition explains how firms operate in a market where 
they are price takers and have no control over market price. The firm’s demand curve is 
horizontal because it can sell any quantity at the prevailing price, which arises due to the 
presence of many buyers and sellers, identical products, and perfect information. The 
derivation of the demand curve through residual demand shows why individual firms face 
highly elastic demand. 

--- Page 19 ---
The theory of profit maximization highlights that firms aim to produce at the level where 
marginal revenue equals marginal cost (MR = MC). In the short run, firms may earn profits, 
incur losses, or break even, but they continue production as long as they can cover variable 
costs. In the long run, firms can freely enter or exit the market, and this adjustment process 
ensures that all firms earn only normal profit. 
Multiple Choice Questions 
1. What defines a perfectly competitive market? 
A. All firms have the ability to influence market prices.  
B. There are many buyers and sellers, and products are identical.  
C. Firms operate with significant market power.  
D. Prices are set by individual firms based on demand. 
Answer: B. There are many buyers and sellers, and products are identical.  
2. Why is a firm considered as a price taker in a perfectly competitive market? 
A. Because it has a unique product that no other firm offers.  
B. Because it can influence the market price through its output.  
C. Because the firm's output is insignificant relative to total market supply.  
D. Because it operates in a monopoly market structure. 
Answer: C. Because the firm's output is insignificant relative to total market supply 
3. In the long run, what happens to firms in a perfectly competitive market that are earning 
supernormal profits? 
A. They will continue to earn supernormal profits indefinitely.  
B. Other firms will enter the market, driving down prices.  

--- Page 20 ---
C. Firms will exit the market to avoid further losses.  
D. They will increase their prices to maximize profits. 
Answer: B. Other firms will enter the market, driving down prices.  
 
4. What is the implication of the horizontal demand curve faced by a firm in perfect 
competition? 
A. The firm can raise its prices without losing customers.  
B. The firm can sell any quantity at the prevailing market price.  
C. Demand for the firm's product is inelastic.  
D. The firm has control over the market supply. 
Answer: B. The firm can sell any quantity at the prevailing market price 
5. What is meant by long-run equilibrium in a perfectly competitive market? 
A. Firms earn supernormal profit due to high demand.  
B. Price equals long-run average cost, resulting in zero economic profit.  
C. Firms will always have the option to exit the market.  
D. The market will fluctuate continuously without stabilizing. 
Answer: B. Price equals long-run average cost, resulting in zero economic profit.

Module IV 
Market Structure 
Unit 18: Perfect Competition 
 
I. Price Taking 
II. Why the Firm’s Demand Curve Is Horizontal  
III. Derivation of a Competitive Firm’s Demand Curve  
IV. Profit Maximization  
V. Short-Run Competitive Profit Maximization  
VI. Long-Run Competitive Profit Maximization 
 
Objectives of the Study: 
After studying this unit, the student should be able to 
- 
understand the market structure Perfect Competition 
 
Perfect Competition 
Perfect competition is a common market structure that has very desirable properties, so it is 
useful to compare other market structures to competition. In this section, we describe the 
properties of competitive firms and markets. 
In general terms, competition refers to firms rivalling with one another to attract customers. 
However, in economics, a market is considered perfectly competitive only when firms are price 
takers, meaning they cannot influence market prices and must accept the price determined by 
market demand and supply. 
Perfect competition represents an ideal market situation where resources are allocated 
efficiently, and no individual buyer or seller has control over the price. 
I. Price Taking 
When most people talk about “competitive firms,” they usually refer to firms that compete or 
rival with one another to attract customers. In this general sense, any market with more than

one firm may be considered competitive. However, in economics, the term “competitive 
market” has a more precise meaning. 
Economists define a market as competitive only when all firms within it are price takers. A 
price-taking firm is one that cannot influence the market price of its product or the prices of 
the inputs it uses. Instead, the price is determined by the overall interaction of market demand 
and supply, and each individual firm must accept this price. 
Why is a firm a price taker? 
A firm becomes a price taker because of the structure of the market in which it operates. In a 
perfectly competitive market: 
 
There are a large number of firms. 
 
Each firm produces only a very small portion of total output. 
 
Products are identical across firms. 
Due to these conditions, no single firm has enough market power to influence price. If one firm 
changes its output, the effect on total market supply is negligible, and therefore the market 
price remains unchanged. 
Role of the Demand Curve 
A key reason why firms are price takers is that they face a perfectly elastic (horizontal) demand 
curve at the prevailing market price. This has several important implications: 
 
The firm can sell any quantity of output at the given market price. 
 
The firm has no incentive to lower its price, because it can already sell all its output at 
the existing price. 
 
The firm cannot increase its price, because buyers would immediately switch to other 
sellers offering the same product. 
Infinitely Elastic Demand 
The demand curve faced by the firm is said to be infinitely elastic. This means: 
 
Even a very small increase in price leads to a complete loss of customers.

 
At the market price, demand is perfectly responsive, allowing the firm to sell any 
quantity. 
For example, consider a farmer selling wheat in a large agricultural market. If the farmer tries 
to charge a higher price than others, buyers will simply purchase wheat from other farmers 
since all wheat is identical. As a result, the farmer has no control over price and must accept 
the prevailing market rate. 
II. Why the Firm’s Demand Curve Is Horizontal  
In a perfectly competitive market, the demand curve faced by an individual firm is perfectly 
elastic, meaning it is a horizontal straight line at the prevailing market price. This occurs 
because firms are price takers and cannot influence the price through their individual actions. 
The horizontal nature of the demand curve is not accidental; it is the result of several important 
characteristics of perfect competition. 
1. Large Number of Buyers and Sellers 
In a perfectly competitive market, there are a large number of buyers and sellers, each of whom 
is very small relative to the overall market. As a result: 
 
No single firm can influence the total market supply. 
 
Any change in the output of a single firm has a negligible effect on market price. 
For example, soybean farmers are price takers because each farmer produces only a tiny 
fraction of total output. Even if one farmer stops producing, the overall market supply changes 
very little, so the market price remains unaffected. 
Thus, each firm must accept the given market price, which leads to a horizontal demand curve. 
2. Identical (Homogeneous) Products 
All firms in perfect competition produce identical or homogeneous products. Consumers 
perceive no difference between goods supplied by different firms. 
 
A buyer does not care which firm supplies the product.

 
If one firm charges a higher price, consumers will immediately switch to other sellers. 
For instance, agricultural products like apples or wheat are considered identical in quality. 
Because of this uniformity, no firm can charge a price above the market level. 
This forces firms to accept the market price, making the demand curve perfectly elastic. 
3. Full Information 
In a perfectly competitive market, buyers and sellers have complete knowledge about: 
 
Prices charged by all firms 
 
Product quality and characteristics 
This transparency ensures that: 
 
Buyers always purchase from the cheapest seller. 
 
Firms cannot charge higher prices without losing all customers. 
If a firm attempts to increase its price, consumers—being fully informed—will shift instantly 
to other firms. Hence, the firm’s demand drops to zero above the market price. 
4. Negligible Transaction Costs 
Transaction costs refer to the costs involved in buying or selling a product, such as time, 
transportation, or legal expenses. 
In perfect competition: 
 
These costs are very low or negligible. 
 
Buyers can easily switch from one seller to another without any inconvenience. 
For example, in commodity markets, buyers can quickly compare prices and make purchases 
with minimal effort. Because switching is so easy, even a slight increase in price by a firm will 
result in a complete loss of demand. This reinforces the horizontal shape of the demand curve. 
5. Free Entry and Exit of Firms

Firms can freely enter or exit the market depending on profit conditions: 
 
If firms earn abnormal profits, new firms enter the market. 
 
Increased competition pushes prices down to the normal level. 
 
If firms incur losses, some firms exit, reducing supply and stabilizing prices. 
This process ensures that: 
 
No firm can sustain a higher price in the long run. 
 
Firms remain price takers at all times. 
A practical example of a nearly perfectly competitive market is the Chicago Mercantile 
Exchange. 
This market exhibits the following features: 
 
Thousands of buyers and sellers participate in trading. 
 
Products such as wheat and other commodities are standardized and identical. 
 
Prices are publicly available, ensuring full information. 
 
Transactions occur quickly with minimal cost. 
 
Entry and exit into trading are relatively easy. 
Because of these conditions, traders in such markets cannot influence prices individually and 
must accept the prevailing market price. 
Deviations from Perfect Competition  
In reality, very few markets satisfy all the strict conditions of perfect competition. Most markets 
deviate from this ideal structure in one way or another. However, even when these deviations 
exist, many markets still behave in a manner similar to perfectly competitive markets, 
especially when there are a large number of firms and strong competition. 
1. Government Restrictions on Entry 
In some markets, the government imposes restrictions that limit the entry of new firms. These 
restrictions may include:

 
Licensing requirements 
 
Zoning laws 
 
Legal regulations 
Such barriers prevent completely free entry and exit, which is a key feature of perfect 
competition. However, if the number of existing firms is still large, individual firms may 
continue to behave as price takers because no single firm has significant control over price. 
2. Presence of Transaction Costs 
In the real world, transaction costs are rarely zero. Buyers and sellers may incur costs such as: 
 
Transportation expenses 
 
Search costs (finding the best price) 
 
Legal or administrative costs 
When transaction costs are high, consumers may not switch sellers even if there is a price 
difference. This gives some firms limited pricing power. However, if transaction costs are 
relatively low, markets can still function close to perfect competition. 
3. Incomplete or Imperfect Information 
Perfect competition assumes that all buyers and sellers have complete information about prices 
and products. In reality: 
 
Consumers may not know all available prices 
 
Information about product quality may be limited 
Despite this, even if only some buyers are well-informed, they can influence the market by 
choosing lower-priced sellers. This competitive pressure prevents firms from significantly 
increasing prices. 
4. Product Differentiation 
In many markets, products are not perfectly identical. Firms may differentiate their products 
through:

 
Branding 
 
Quality differences 
 
Packaging 
This reduces the degree of competition and gives firms some control over pricing. However, if 
products are still close substitutes, competition remains strong. 
5. Limited Mobility of Resources 
Factors of production such as labor and capital may not move freely due to: 
 
Skill differences 
 
Geographical constraints 
 
Institutional barriers 
This restricts the flexibility assumed in perfect competition. Even so, in industries where 
mobility is relatively high, firms behave more like price takers. 
 
III. Derivation of a Competitive Firm’s Demand Curve  
The demand curve faced by an individual firm in a competitive market is derived from the 
concept of residual demand. Residual demand refers to the portion of total market demand that 
remains after accounting for the supply provided by all other firms in the market. 
In other words, a firm can only sell what other firms do not supply at a given price. 
Residual Demand Concept 
A firm faces a residual demand curve defined as: 
Dr(p) = D(p) - So(p) 
Where: 
 
Dr(p) = Residual demand for the firm 
 
D(p) = Total market demand

 
So(p) = Supply of all other firms 
This equation shows that the demand available to an individual firm depends on both the total 
market demand and the quantity supplied by competing firms. 
The concept of residual demand can be understood step by step: 
 
A firm sells its product only to those consumers who have not already purchased from 
other firms. 
 
At high prices, other firms are willing to supply a large quantity. If their supply fully 
satisfies market demand, the residual demand for the firm becomes zero. 
 
At lower prices, other firms supply less than the total market demand. The remaining 
unmet demand becomes available to the individual firm. 
Thus, the firm’s demand is not the total market demand, but only the leftover demand after 
other firms have supplied their share. 
The residual demand curve is derived by comparing: 
 
The market demand curve, and 
 
The supply curve of other firms 
At each price level: 
 
Subtract the quantity supplied by other firms from total market demand. 
 
The remaining quantity represents the demand faced by the individual firm. 
Graphically, the residual demand curve is the horizontal difference between the market demand 
curve and the supply curve of other firms as shown in the figure 18.1. 
Figure 18.1: Residual Demand Curve

The market demand that is not met by other sellers at any given price. The firm’s residual 
demand function, Dr(p), shows the quantity demanded from the firm at price p. A firm sells 
only to people who have not already purchased the good from another seller. We can determine 
how much demand is left for a particular firm at each possible price using the market demand 
curve and the supply curve for all other firms in the market. The quantity the market demands 
is a function of the price: 
Q = D(p) 
The supply curve of the other firms is So(p). The residual demand function equals the market 
demand function, D(p), minus the supply function of all other firms: 
Dr(p) = D(p) - So(p) 
At prices so high that the amount supplied by other firms, So(p), is greater than the quantity 
demanded by the market, D(p), the residual quantity demanded, Dr(p), is zero. In Figure 18.1 
we derive the residual demand for a Canadian manufacturing firm that produces metal chairs. 
Panel b shows the market demand curve, D, and the supply of all but one manufacturing firm, 
So. At p = $66 per chair, the supply of other firms, 500 units (where one unit is 1,000 metal 
chairs) per year, exactly equals the market demand (panel b), so the residual quantity demanded 
of the remaining firm (panel a) is zero. At prices below $66, the other chair manufacturers are 
not willing to supply as much as the market demands. At p = $63, for example, the market 
demand is 527 units, but other firms want to supply only 434 units. As a result, the residual 
quantity demanded from the individual firm at p = $63 is 93 (= 527 - 434) units. Thus, the 
residual demand curve at any given price is the horizontal difference between the market 
demand curve and the supply curve of the other firms. The residual demand curve the firm 
faces in panel a is much flatter than the market demand curve in panel b. As a result, the 
elasticity of the residual demand curve is much higher than the market elasticity. If the market 
has n identical firms, the elasticity of demand, εi, facing Firm i is 
εi = nε - (n - 1)ηo,

where ε is the market elasticity of demand (a negative number), ηo is the elasticity of supply of 
each of the other firms (typically a positive number), and n - 1 is the number of other firms. As 
equation εi = nε - (n - 1)ηo shows, a firm’s residual demand curve is more elastic the more 
firms, n, are in the market, the more elastic the market demand, ε, and the larger the elasticity 
of supply of the other firms, ηo. The residual demand elasticity, εi, must be at least as elastic as 
nε if the supply curve slopes up so that the second term makes the estimate more elastic. Thus, 
using nε as an approximation is conservative. For example, even though the estimated market 
elasticity of demand for soybeans is very inelastic at about ε = -0.2, because n = 107,000, the 
residual demand facing a single soybean farm must be at least nε = 107,000 × (-0.2) = -21,400, 
which is extremely elastic. 
Thus, we can say that the residual demand curve has the following characteristics: 
 
It is flatter (more elastic) than the market demand curve. 
 
As the number of firms increases, each firm’s share of the market becomes smaller. 
 
Consequently, the residual demand curve becomes more elastic. 
 
In the case of a very large number of firms, the curve becomes perfectly horizontal, 
indicating perfectly elastic demand. 
This explains why firms in perfect competition are price takers. 
IV. Profit Maximization 
Economists generally assume that all firms aim to maximize profit. This assumption is based 
on two main reasons: 
 
Many businesspeople explicitly state that profit maximization is their objective. 
 
Firms that fail to maximize profit are likely to incur losses and eventually be forced out 
of the market. 
Thus, profit maximization is considered the primary goal of firms in economic theory. 
Meaning of Profit 
A firm’s profit π, is defined as the difference between its total revenue R and total cost C: 
π = R - C

 
If (π > 0) → Profit 
 
If (π < 0) → Loss 
Economic Cost vs Business Cost 
Economists measure cost as opportunity cost, which includes: 
 
Explicit costs (wages, materials, rent) 
 
Implicit costs (forgone income, owner’s time) 
This leads to a difference between: 
 
Business profit (accounting profit) 
 
Economic profit 
Example: 
Suppose a person earns ₹20,000 from their own business. If they could earn ₹25,000 working 
elsewhere, then: 
 
Economic profit = 20,000 − 25,000 = –₹5,000 (loss) 
Thus, ignoring opportunity cost can lead to incorrect decisions. 
A firm must make two key decisions for profit maximisation: 
1. Output Decision 
What level of output q* maximizes profit? 
2. Shutdown Decision 
Should the firm produce or shut down? 
Profit Maximization Rules 
Rule 1: The firm produces the output level where profit is maximum. 
Rule 2: The firm produces where marginal profit = 0.

Rule 3: MR(q) = MC(q) 
Where: 
 
MR = Marginal Revenue 
 
MC = Marginal Cost 
That is, 
 
If MR > MC → Increase output 
 
If MR < MC → Reduce output 
 
If MR = MC → Profit is maximized 
Shutdown Rule  
The shutdown rule is an important concept in economics that helps a firm decide whether it 
should continue production or temporarily cease operations in order to minimize losses. This 
decision depends on the relationship between the firm’s revenue and its costs, and it differs 
between the short run and the long run. 
In the short run, a firm faces two types of costs namely fixed costs and variable costs. Fixed 
costs, such as rent, machinery, and equipment, are considered sunk costs because they must be 
paid regardless of whether the firm produces any output. Since these costs cannot be recovered, 
they are irrelevant when making the shutdown decision. Instead, the firm focuses only on 
variable costs, which include expenses like wages, raw materials, and electricity—costs that 
can be avoided if production stops. If the firm’s total revenue is greater than or equal to its 
variable cost, it should continue producing, even if it is making an overall loss. This is because 
the firm is covering all its variable costs and contributing something toward its fixed costs, 
thereby reducing its total loss. However, if the firm’s revenue falls below its variable cost, it 
means that the firm cannot even cover the costs that could be avoided by shutting down. In 
such a situation, continuing production would increase losses, so the firm should temporarily 
shut down. So in the short run shut down only if:  Revenue < Variable Cost. 
In the long run, the shutdown decision becomes simpler because all costs are variable and 
avoidable. There are no fixed or sunk costs, as the firm has enough time to adjust all inputs, 
sell assets, or exit the industry completely. Therefore, the firm must ensure that its total revenue

covers all its costs. If the firm is unable to do so and incurs any economic loss, it will choose 
to shut down and exit the market. Unlike in the short run, there is no justification for continuing 
production at a loss because all costs can be avoided. 
V. Short-Run Competitive Profit Maximization 
Meaning of Short Run  
The short run in economics refers to a period of time during which at least one factor of 
production remains fixed and cannot be changed. This fixed factor is usually capital, such as 
machinery, buildings, or equipment, which cannot be increased or reduced quickly due to time 
and cost constraints. Because of this limitation, firms can adjust only some inputs—like labor 
or raw materials—while others remain constant. In the short run, firms also cannot freely enter 
or exit the market. New firms cannot quickly enter because setting up production facilities takes 
time, and existing firms cannot completely leave the market since they are tied to fixed assets. 
However, they may choose to temporarily stop production if conditions are unfavourable. Thus, 
the short run is characterized by limited flexibility in production decisions and constraints on 
market participation. 
Output Decision in Short Run  
In the short run, a firm operating under perfect competition determines its level of output based 
on the goal of profit maximization. Since the firm is a price taker, it has no control over the 
market price and must accept the price determined by market demand and supply. As a result, 
the firm’s price (P) is equal to its marginal revenue (MR). This means that every additional 
unit sold adds the same amount to revenue, equal to the market price. Therefore, the profit-
maximizing condition for a competitive firm becomes: 
MC(q) = p 
This condition implies that the firm will adjust its level of output until its marginal cost (MC) 
equals the market price. If the marginal cost of producing an additional unit is less than the 
price (MC < P), the firm can increase its profit by producing more, because the revenue from 
selling that unit exceeds its cost. On the other hand, if the marginal cost is greater than the price 
(MC > P), the firm should reduce its output, as producing extra units would add more to cost 
than to revenue, thereby reducing profit. Profit is maximized only when MC = P, because at

this point, the additional revenue from producing one more unit exactly equals the additional 
cost, and there is no further gain from changing output. Thus, in the short run, a competitive 
firm carefully adjusts its production level to this equilibrium condition in order to achieve 
maximum profit or minimum loss. 
Profit or Loss in the Short Run and Short-Run Supply Curve  
In the short run, a firm operating under perfect competition may find itself in different profit 
situations depending on market conditions and its cost structure. The firm may earn 
supernormal (abnormal) profit when its total revenue exceeds total cost, or normal profit when 
revenue just equals total cost, covering both explicit and implicit costs. However, the firm may 
also incur losses when total cost exceeds total revenue. Despite this possibility, a firm does not 
immediately shut down when it incurs losses in the short run. This is because fixed costs, such 
as rent and machinery, are unavoidable in the short run. As long as the firm’s revenue is 
sufficient to cover its variable costs, it will continue production, since doing so allows it to 
cover part of its fixed costs and thereby reduce overall losses. The firm will only shut down if 
its revenue falls below variable costs. 
The short-run supply curve of a competitive firm is derived from its marginal cost (MC) curve, 
but only the portion that lies above the average variable cost (AVC) curve. This is because the 
firm will produce only when price (which equals marginal revenue) is at least equal to AVC. 
If the price falls below AVC, the firm cannot cover its variable costs and will shut down. Thus, 
the MC curve above AVC represents the firm’s willingness to supply output at different price 
levels. 
The key insight from this analysis is that in the short run, firms have limited flexibility due to 
fixed costs. As a result, they may continue operating even when they are making losses, 
provided they can cover their variable costs. Fixed costs cannot be avoided in the short run, so 
firms focus on minimizing losses rather than immediately exiting the market. 
VI. Long-Run Competitive Profit Maximization 
Meaning of Long Run  
The long run in economics refers to a period of time sufficiently long for a firm to adjust all its 
factors of production. Unlike the short run, where at least one factor remains fixed, in the long

run all inputs are variable, meaning firms can change the scale of production by increasing or 
decreasing labor, capital, machinery, and plant size. Because of this flexibility, firms can fully 
adapt to changes in market conditions. 
Another important feature of the long run is that firms can freely enter or exit the market. If 
existing firms are earning profits, new firms are attracted to the industry, increasing 
competition. On the other hand, if firms are incurring losses, some will leave the market. This 
process continues until only normal profits are earned. 
In the long run, no fixed costs remain, because all costs can be adjusted or avoided. Firms are 
not bound by past investments, and they can reorganize production or completely shut down if 
it is not profitable. As a result, the long run represents a period of full flexibility and adjustment, 
where firms make decisions that ensure efficiency and long-term sustainability. 
Output Decision in Long Run  
In the long run, a firm determines its level of output using the same fundamental profit-
maximization rule as in the short run. The firm aims to produce at the level where its marginal 
revenue (MR) equals marginal cost (MC), since this is the point at which profit is maximized. 
In a perfectly competitive market, the firm is a price taker, meaning it cannot influence the 
market price and must accept it as given. Therefore, the firm’s marginal revenue is equal to the 
market price. 
MR = MC 
Since: 
MR = P 
It follows that: 
MC = P 
This means that in the long run, the firm will adjust its output level until the marginal cost of 
producing an additional unit equals the market price. If the marginal cost is less than the price, 
the firm can increase profit by expanding production. If the marginal cost is greater than the 
price, the firm should reduce output to avoid losses. The equilibrium is reached when MC

equals price, ensuring that the firm is producing the most efficient level of output. Thus, even 
in the long run, the condition MC = P remains the key rule guiding a competitive firm’s output 
decision. 
Shutdown Decision in Long Run  
The shutdown decision in the long run is relatively simple compared to the short run because 
all costs are variable and avoidable. Unlike the short run, there are no fixed or sunk costs that 
the firm is forced to bear. This means the firm has complete flexibility to adjust its inputs, scale 
of production, or even exit the market entirely. As a result, the firm must ensure that its total 
revenue is sufficient to cover all its costs in order to continue operating. 
If a firm finds that it is incurring any economic loss, meaning its total revenue is less than its 
total cost, it will choose to shut down and exit the market. Continuing production in such a 
situation would not be rational, since the firm can avoid all costs by ceasing operations. 
Therefore, in the long run, only firms that are able to earn at least normal profit (where revenue 
equals total cost) will remain in the market. Firms that fail to do so will exit, ensuring that 
resources are allocated efficiently over time. 
Long-Run Supply Curve  
In the long run, the supply curve of a perfectly competitive firm is derived from its long-run 
marginal cost (LRMC) curve, but only the portion that lies above the long-run average cost 
(LRAC) curve. This is because, in the long run, all costs are variable and the firm must cover 
all its costs to remain in business. The firm will choose to produce only when the market price 
is at least equal to its average cost; otherwise, it will incur losses and exit the market. 
A profit-maximizing firm determines its output where price equals marginal cost (P = MC). In 
the long run, this condition becomes P = LRMC, and the firm supplies output only if this price 
is also sufficient to cover the average cost. Therefore, the relevant portion of the LRMC curve 
is the segment that lies above the LRAC curve, as this ensures that the firm earns at least normal 
profit. 
If the market price is below the LRAC, the firm cannot cover its total costs and will shut down 
in the long run. On the other hand, if the price is equal to the minimum point of the LRAC 
curve, the firm earns zero economic profit (normal profit) and continues operating. Thus, the

long-run supply curve reflects the firm’s willingness to supply output at different price levels 
while ensuring long-term sustainability and efficiency. 
Entry and Exit of Firms  
In a perfectly competitive market, the number of firms in the industry is determined by the 
processes of entry and exit, which occur in response to profit or loss. Entry of firms takes place 
when existing firms in the market are earning supernormal (abnormal) profits. These high 
profits act as an incentive for new firms to enter the industry, as they expect to earn similar 
returns. As new firms enter, the total market supply increases, which leads to a fall in market 
price and a reduction in profits. 
On the other hand, exit of firms occurs when firms in the market are incurring losses. Losses 
signal that resources are not being used efficiently, so some firms choose to leave the industry 
to avoid further losses. As firms exit, the total market supply decreases, which causes the 
market price to rise and reduces the losses of the remaining firms. 
This continuous process of entry and exit ensures that, in the long run, firms earn only normal 
profit (zero economic profit). It also helps maintain equilibrium in the market by adjusting 
supply in response to changes in profitability. 
Long-Run Equilibrium  
In a perfectly competitive market, long-run equilibrium is achieved when firms reach a position 
where price equals marginal revenue, marginal cost, and long-run average cost: 
P = MR = MC = LRAC 
At this point, firms are producing at the most efficient level of output, where the cost of 
producing an additional unit (MC) is exactly equal to the revenue earned from it (MR), and this 
is also equal to the market price. Since price is equal to long-run average cost (LRAC), firms 
are able to cover all their costs, including both explicit and implicit (opportunity) costs. 
One of the key implications of this equilibrium is that firms earn zero economic profit, also 
known as normal profit. This does not mean firms are making no money; rather, it means they 
are earning just enough to keep their resources in the current use, with no extra incentive for

new firms to enter or existing firms to leave the market. As a result, there is no tendency for 
entry or exit, and the market remains stable. 
Another important implication is that the price equals the minimum point of the average cost 
curve, which indicates that firms are operating at the most efficient scale of production. This 
leads to an efficient allocation of resources, where goods are produced at the lowest possible 
cost and supplied at a price that reflects this efficiency. Thus, long-run equilibrium in perfect 
competition ensures both productive efficiency and overall economic efficiency in the market. 
Adjustment Process  
The adjustment process in a perfectly competitive market explains how the forces of entry and 
exit bring the market toward long-run equilibrium. When firms in the market are earning 
supernormal profits, it signals that the industry is highly profitable. This attracts new firms to 
enter the market, as they expect to earn similar profits. As more firms enter, the overall market 
supply increases, which leads to a fall in market price. This process continues until the extra 
profits are eliminated and firms earn only normal profit. 
On the other hand, when firms are incurring losses, it indicates that the market is not profitable. 
As a result, some firms exit the market to avoid further losses. The exit of firms reduces the 
total market supply, which in turn causes the market price to rise. This rise in price helps the 
remaining firms recover their costs. The process of exit continues until losses are eliminated 
and firms again earn normal profit. 
Thus, the adjustment process ensures that in the long run, the market stabilizes at a point where 
firms earn zero economic profit, with no incentive for further entry or exit. 
Conclusion 
In conclusion, the concept of perfect competition explains how firms operate in a market where 
they are price takers and have no control over market price. The firm’s demand curve is 
horizontal because it can sell any quantity at the prevailing price, which arises due to the 
presence of many buyers and sellers, identical products, and perfect information. The 
derivation of the demand curve through residual demand shows why individual firms face 
highly elastic demand.

The theory of profit maximization highlights that firms aim to produce at the level where 
marginal revenue equals marginal cost (MR = MC). In the short run, firms may earn profits, 
incur losses, or break even, but they continue production as long as they can cover variable 
costs. In the long run, firms can freely enter or exit the market, and this adjustment process 
ensures that all firms earn only normal profit. 
Multiple Choice Questions 
1. What defines a perfectly competitive market? 
A. All firms have the ability to influence market prices.  
B. There are many buyers and sellers, and products are identical.  
C. Firms operate with significant market power.  
D. Prices are set by individual firms based on demand. 
Answer: B. There are many buyers and sellers, and products are identical.  
2. Why is a firm considered as a price taker in a perfectly competitive market? 
A. Because it has a unique product that no other firm offers.  
B. Because it can influence the market price through its output.  
C. Because the firm's output is insignificant relative to total market supply.  
D. Because it operates in a monopoly market structure. 
Answer: C. Because the firm's output is insignificant relative to total market supply 
3. In the long run, what happens to firms in a perfectly competitive market that are earning 
supernormal profits? 
A. They will continue to earn supernormal profits indefinitely.  
B. Other firms will enter the market, driving down prices.

C. Firms will exit the market to avoid further losses.  
D. They will increase their prices to maximize profits. 
Answer: B. Other firms will enter the market, driving down prices.  
 
4. What is the implication of the horizontal demand curve faced by a firm in perfect 
competition? 
A. The firm can raise its prices without losing customers.  
B. The firm can sell any quantity at the prevailing market price.  
C. Demand for the firm's product is inelastic.  
D. The firm has control over the market supply. 
Answer: B. The firm can sell any quantity at the prevailing market price 
5. What is meant by long-run equilibrium in a perfectly competitive market? 
A. Firms earn supernormal profit due to high demand.  
B. Price equals long-run average cost, resulting in zero economic profit.  
C. Firms will always have the option to exit the market.  
D. The market will fluctuate continuously without stabilizing. 
Answer: B. Price equals long-run average cost, resulting in zero economic profit.

Unit 19: Monopoly 
I. Monopoly Profit Maximization  
II. Market Power 
 
Objectives of the Study: 
After studying this unit, the student should be able to 
 
-understand the Monopoly market structure 
Monopoly 
A monopoly is a market structure in which a single firm is the only supplier of a product that 
has no close substitutes. This means consumers do not have alternative choices, so the 
monopolist has significant control over the market. Monopolies have existed since ancient 
times. For example, the Greek philosopher Thales once controlled olive presses, and ancient 
Egyptian rulers-controlled food supply. In modern times, governments may also create 
monopolies by granting patents, which give firms exclusive rights to produce and sell a product 
for a certain period. Companies like Apple initially had near-monopoly power with products 
such as the iPod and iPad. 
Unlike firms in perfect competition, a monopoly is a price maker, not a price taker. This means 
it has the power to influence or set the price of its product. Since the monopolist is the only 
seller, its output is equal to the total market supply, and it faces the market demand curve, 
which is downward sloping. This downward slope indicates that if the monopolist increases 
the price, the quantity demanded will decrease, but not fall to zero. 
Because of this, a monopoly maximizes its profit by producing at the level where marginal 
revenue equals marginal cost (MR = MC) and then charging the highest price consumers are 
willing to pay for that quantity, based on the demand curve. As a result, the monopoly sets a 
price higher than marginal cost, unlike in perfect competition where price equals marginal cost. 
This leads to important consequences: 
 
Consumers pay higher prices 

--- Page 2 ---
 
Quantity sold is lower than in a competitive market 
 
There is a loss of economic efficiency (deadweight loss) 
Thus, monopoly results in reduced consumer welfare compared to perfect competition, as 
goods are underproduced and overpriced. 
I. Monopoly Profit Maximization  
All firms, including competitive firms and monopolies, maximize their profits by setting 
marginal revenue equal to marginal cost. 
Marginal Revenue 
A firm’s marginal revenue curve depends on its demand curve. A monopoly’s marginal 
revenue curve lies below its demand curve at any positive quantity because its demand curve 
is downward sloping. 
Marginal Revenue and Price  
A firm’s demand curve shows the price, p, it receives for selling a given quantity, q. The price 
is the average revenue the firm receives, so a firm’s revenue is R = pq. A firm’s marginal 
revenue, MR, is the change in its revenue from selling one more unit. A firm that earns ΔR 
more revenue when it sells Δq extra units of output has a marginal revenue of MR = ΔR/Δq. 
Figure 19.1: Demand Curve 
 
 
If the firm sells exactly one more unit, Δq = 1, its marginal revenue is MR = ΔR. Although the 
marginal revenue curve is horizontal for a competitive firm, it is downward sloping for a 
monopoly. The competitive firm in panel a of figure 19.1 faces a horizontal demand curve at 
the market price, p1. Because its demand curve is horizontal, the competitive firm can sell 

--- Page 3 ---
another unit of output without dropping its price. As a result, the marginal revenue it receives 
from selling the last unit of output is the market price. 
Initially, the competitive firm sells q units of output at the market price of p1, so its revenue, 
R1, is area A, which is a rectangle that is p1 × q. If the firm sells one more unit, its revenue is 
R2 = A + B, where area B is p1 × 1 = p1. The competitive firm’s marginal revenue equals the 
market price: 
ΔR = R2 - R1 = (A + B) - A = B = p1. 
A monopoly faces a downward-sloping market demand curve, as in panel b of figure 19.1. 
(We’ve called the number of units of output a firm sells q and the output of all the firms in a 
market, or market output, Q. Because a monopoly is the only firm in the market, q and Q do 
not differ, so we use Q to describe both the firm’s and the market’s output.) The monopoly, 
which is initially selling Q units at p1, can sell one extra unit only if the price falls to p2.  
The monopoly’s initial revenue, p1 × Q, is R1 = A + C. When it sells the extra unit, its revenue, 
p2 × (Q + 1), is R2 = A + B. Thus, its marginal revenue is 
ΔR = R2 - R1 = (A + B) - (A + C) = B - C. 
The monopoly sells the extra unit of output at the new price, p2, so its extra revenue is 
B = p2 × 1 = p2. 
 The monopoly loses the difference between the new price and the original price, Δp = (p2 - 
p1), on the Q units it originally sold:  
C = Δp × Q. 
Thus, the monopoly’s marginal revenue, B - C = p2 - C, is less than the price it charges by an 
amount equal to area C. The competitive firm in panel a does not lose an area C from selling 
an extra unit because its demand curve is horizontal. It is the downward slope of the 
monopoly’s demand curve that causes its marginal revenue to be less than its price. 
 
Marginal Revenue Curve  
Thus, the monopoly’s marginal revenue curve lies below the demand curve at every positive 
quantity. In general, the relationship between the marginal revenue and demand curves depends 
on the shape of the demand curve. For all linear demand curves, the relationship between the 
marginal revenue and demand curve is the same. The marginal revenue curve is a straight line 
that starts at the same point on the vertical (price) axis as the demand curve but has twice the 
slope of the demand curve, so the marginal revenue curve hits the horizontal (quantity) axis at 
half the quantity as the demand curve.  
Deriving the Marginal Revenue Curve  

--- Page 4 ---
To derive the monopoly’s marginal revenue curve, we write an equation summarizing the 
relationship between price and marginal revenue that panel b of Figure 19.1 illustrates. For a 
monopoly to increase its output by ΔQ, the monopoly lowers its price per unit by Δp/ΔQ, which 
is the slope of the demand curve. By lowering its price, the monopoly loses (Δp/ΔQ) ×Q on the 
units it originally sold at the higher price (area C), but it earns an additional p on the extra 
output it now sells (area B). Thus, the monopoly’s marginal revenue is 
MR =  p + Δp
ΔQ  Q 
Because the slope of the monopoly’s inverse demand curve, Δp/ΔQ, is negative, the last term 
in the equation (Δp/ΔQ) Q, is negative. This equation confirms that the price is greater than the 
marginal revenue, which equals p plus a negative term. 
 
Marginal Revenue and Price Elasticity of Demand  
The marginal revenue at any given quantity depends on the demand curve’s height (the price) 
and shape. The shape of the demand curve at a particular quantity is described by the price 
elasticity of demand, ε = (ΔQ/Q)/(Δp/p) < 0, which is the percentage by which quantity 
demanded falls as the price increases by 1%. 
At a given quantity, the marginal revenue equals the price times a term involving the elasticity 
of demand: 
𝑀𝑅= 𝑝(1 + 1
𝜀) 
According to this equation, marginal revenue is closer to price as demand becomes more 
elastic. Where the demand curve hits the price axis (Q = 0), the demand curve is perfectly 
elastic, so the marginal revenue equals price: MR = p. Where the demand elasticity is unitary, 
ε = -1, marginal revenue is zero: MR = p[1 + 1/(-1)] = 0. 
Marginal revenue is negative where the demand curve is inelastic, -1 < ε ≤ 0. 
Choosing Price or Quantity 
Any firm maximizes its profit by operating where its marginal revenue equals its marginal cost. 
Unlike a competitive firm, a monopoly can adjust its price, so it has a choice of setting its price 
or its quantity to maximize its profit. (A competitive firm sets its quantity to maximize profit 
because it cannot affect market price.) 
The monopoly is constrained by the market demand curve. Because the demand curve slopes 
down, the monopoly faces a trade-off between a higher price and a lower quantity or a lower 
price and a higher quantity. The monopoly chooses the point on the demand curve that 

--- Page 5 ---
maximizes its profit. Unfortunately for the monopoly, it cannot set both its quantity and its 
price. If it could do so, the monopoly would choose an extremely high price and an extremely 
high output level—above its demand curve—and would become exceedingly wealthy. If the 
monopoly sets its price, the demand curve determines how much output it sells. If the monopoly 
picks an output level, the demand curve determines the price. Because the monopoly wants to 
operate at the price and output at which its profit is maximized, it chooses the same profit-
maximizing solution whether it sets the price or output. In the rest of this chapter, we assume 
that the monopoly sets quantity 
Graphical Approach 
All firms, including monopolies, use a two-step analysis to determine the output level that 
maximizes their profit. First, the firm determines the output, Q*, at which it makes the highest 
possible profit—the output at which its marginal revenue equals its marginal cost. Second, the 
firm decides whether to produce Q* or shut down. 
 
Figure 19.2: Monopoly Profit Maximisation 
 
 
In the figure 19.2 Panel b shows the corresponding profit curve. The profit curve reaches its 
maximum at 6 units of output, where marginal profit—the slope of the profit curve—is zero. 

--- Page 6 ---
Because marginal profit =marginal revenue - marginal cost, marginal profit is zero where 
marginal revenue equals marginal cost. In panel a, marginal revenue equals marginal cost at 6 
units. The price on the demand curve at that quantity is 18. Thus, the monopoly maximizes its 
profit at point e, where it sells 6 units per day at a price of 18 per unit. 
Why does the monopoly maximize its profit by producing where its marginal revenue equals 
its marginal cost? At smaller quantities, the monopoly’s marginal revenue is greater than its 
marginal cost, so its marginal profit is positive—the profit curve is upward sloping. By 
increasing its output, the monopoly raises its profit. Similarly, at quantities greater than 6 units, 
the monopoly’s marginal cost is greater than its marginal revenue, so its marginal 
profit is negative, and the monopoly can increase its profit by reducing its output. The marginal 
revenue curve is positive where the elasticity of demand is elastic, is zero at the quantity where
